title: ED length-of-stay rise at Halden Valley Community Hospital

organization.size: 400 licensed beds (388 staffed adult beds), 36-room emergency department, approx. 2,300 staff

presentingRequest: Our emergency department length of stay for admitted patients has gone from 4.1 hours to 7.3 hours in less than a year, and it is now the worst number on our board quality scorecard. The ED Director and I are clear that the cause is ED nurse understaffing: our nurses are overwhelmed, patients are leaving without being seen, and morale is falling. We want your help building the business case for the board to approve eight travel nurses for the ED this quarter and a longer-term ED recruitment plan. - Chief Nursing Officer, Halden Valley Community Hospital

evidence.text: "Our ED length of stay went from 4.1 to 7.3 hours in under a year, and the reason is simple: we do not have enough ED nurses. The nurses tell me every day they are drowning, patients wait in the lobby, and people walk out. I have a quote for eight travel nurses for 13 weeks and I want the board to approve it in November. I don't think we need a study to know nurses are short."

"The front end is a mess. Door-to-provider is up, left-without-being-seen has doubled, and my nurses are carrying four or five patients when the grid says three or four. We lost two experienced nurses to the university hospital in the spring. More nurses on the floor is the fastest fix I can see. The rooms are full every afternoon."

evidence.source: ED quality dashboard, board scorecard extract (prepared 2026-10-06)
evidence.text: Headline measure: median arrival-to-departure time for ED patients admitted to an inpatient bed (the measure reported on the board quality scorecard). Q4 2025: 4.1 h; Q1 2026: 4.9 h; Q2 2026: 6.8 h; Q3 2026: 7.3 h. ED visits per month (quarter average): Q4 2025 5,210; Q3 2026 5,260. Admission rate from ED: 27% in both quarters. Share of visits triaged ESI level 1-2 (highest acuity): 31% vs 32%. Median arrival-to-departure for non-admitted (treat-and-release) patients: 2.9 h vs 3.1 h.

evidence.source: Nursing finance, ED productive-hours and staffing report (Q4 2025 vs Q3 2026)
evidence.text: ED registered-nurse productive hours per ED visit: 2.61 (Q4 2025), 2.58 (Q1 2026), 2.63 (Q2 2026), 2.64 (Q3 2026). ED RN vacancy rate: 11% (Dec 2025) vs 9% (Sep 2026); two RN resignations in April 2026 were backfilled by agency staff within three weeks. Share of shifts staffed at or above the ED staffing grid: 96% (Q4 2025) vs 97% (Q3 2026). Hours are drawn from payroll and agency invoices, not from self-reported schedules.

evidence.source: Decision-support analyst, ED interval decomposition for admitted patients (2026-10-09)
evidence.text: For admitted ED patients, median arrival-to-admit-decision (ED work-up) time: 2.7 h (Q4 2025) vs 2.9 h (Q3 2026). Median admit-decision-to-ED-departure (boarding) time: 1.4 h vs 4.4 h. Of the 3.2 h increase in the headline measure, approximately 3.0 h falls in the boarding interval. Boarding is timestamped by the bed-management system (decision order to patient physically leaving the ED), independent of nursing documentation.

evidence.source: Hospitalist group memo 'Revised daily rounding structure' (effective 2026-03-02)
evidence.text: Effective 2 March 2026, hospitalist rounding on the four adult medical wards (3 East, 3 West, 4 East, 4 West) starts at 09:30 after an 08:00-09:30 multidisciplinary teaching and case-review meeting, replacing the previous 07:00 start. Rounding order is changed to 'new admissions first, then established patients'. Rationale stated: reduce early-morning workload cited in 2025 exit interviews and support teaching. Surgical wards (5 East, 5 West) are rounded by surgical teams and are not covered by this memo.

"Since March we see the new admissions first because they are sickest; by the time we get to the patients going home it is usually after lunch, and then the discharge order, the prescriptions and the summary take time. I know discharges have drifted later. But the old 7 a.m. start was a big reason three hospitalists left in 2025, and I can't go back to that without losing people."

evidence.source: Bed-management system, inpatient discharge timing report (Jan-Feb 2026 vs Apr-Sep 2026)
evidence.text: Hospitalist-covered medical wards: discharges with patient departure before 12:00 fell from 29% (Jan-Feb 2026) to 9% (Apr-Sep 2026); discharges departing after 15:00 rose from 24% to 58%; median discharge-order time moved from 11:50 to 15:25. Surgical wards over the same periods: departures before 12:00 33% vs 31%; median discharge-order time 11:30 vs 11:45. Median discharge-order-to-departure time on medical wards: 1.5 h vs 1.6 h.

evidence.source: Bed-management system, monthly boarding and capacity series (Jan-Sep 2026)
evidence.text: Median ED boarding time for admitted patients by month: Jan 1.4 h, Feb 1.4 h, Mar 3.1 h, Apr 4.2 h, May 4.3 h, Jun 4.4 h, Jul 4.4 h, Aug 4.3 h, Sep 4.6 h. Boarded patients present in the ED peak between 14:00 and 20:00. Staffed adult inpatient beds: 388 in both Q4 2025 and Q3 2026. Midnight census occupancy: 87% vs 88%. Inpatient average length of stay: 4.8 days vs 4.8 days. Medical-ward boarders account for 81% of all boarding hours in Q3 2026.

evidence.source: 4 West unit manager and quality analyst, 'Early-discharge huddle pilot' report (2026-10-08)
evidence.text: Pilot on 4 West (medical, 34 beds) from 10 Aug to 2 Oct 2026. On huddle days, at 09:30, when rounding starts after the 08:00 teaching meeting (which continued unchanged), the charge nurse, the 4 West case manager and the rounding hospitalist agree the list of likely discharges; those patients are seen first, before the new-admission round, and discharge orders are written before noon where possible. The huddle could only run when the rounding hospitalist on 4 West was one of three physicians trained in the protocol; this happened on 24 of 40 weekdays. The case manager prepares the candidate list the afternoon before. Outcomes, huddle vs non-huddle weekdays on 4 West: departures before 12:00 38% vs 11%; median discharge-order time 11:40 vs 15:10; median boarding time for ED patients assigned to a 4 West bed 2.3 h vs 4.6 h.

Which weekdays were huddle days was set by the hospitalist rotation, generated by the group's scheduling software in June 2026 before the pilot was designed. Huddle vs non-huddle weekdays: ED arrivals per day 171 vs 173; ED admissions per day 46 vs 47; 4 West 07:00 census 31.2 vs 31.0. On the same huddle days, median boarding for patients assigned to the other three medical wards was 4.5 h vs 4.4 h on non-huddle days. Before the pilot (Jun-Jul 2026), on days when one of the three later-trained hospitalists rounded on 4 West, departures before 12:00 were 10% vs 9% on other days.

"It's not that we can't get nurses on the schedule - most days we're at grid. It's that by mid-afternoon nine to twelve of our 36 rooms have admitted patients sitting in them waiting for a bed upstairs. Those patients still need meds, vitals, and turns, so my nurses are doing inpatient care and there are no rooms for the people in the lobby. Mornings are usually fine."

evidence.source: ED nursing engagement pulse survey, anonymous (Sep 2026, n=58 of 71, vs Nov 2025, n=55)
evidence.text: Agree 'my workload is manageable most shifts': 59% (Nov 2025) vs 32% (Sep 2026). Intent to leave within 12 months: 14% vs 22%. Most frequent free-text themes in 2026: 'holding admitted patients' (31 comments), 'no rooms for new patients' (19), 'need more staff' (17), 'afternoons are unsafe' (12).

Median door-to-provider time: 22 min (Q4 2025) vs 34 min (Q3 2026). Left without being seen: 1.6% vs 3.4% of visits. The advanced-practice provider-in-triage shift (11:00-23:00), which saw patients in the triage area, was discontinued on 1 May 2026 for budget reasons. Front-end metrics are reported quarterly only; no monthly or hourly series has been produced.

"From 1 September we went from six evening bed-cleaning attendants to four because of a budget freeze. Bed turnaround might be a bit slower in the evenings, I honestly don't know - our turnaround reporting has been down since the July system migration, so I don't have numbers after June."

evidence.source: CFO memo to executive team, 'Funding options for ED travel nurse contract' (2026-10-22)
evidence.text: Eight travel RNs for 13 weeks: $1.46M. Proposed funding: defer filling the two vacant medical-ward case manager positions until April 2027 and reallocate budgeted salary. Current medical-ward case manager coverage is one per 22 patients against a target of one per 15; 4 West's case manager would be reassigned to cover 4 East as well if the deferral proceeds.

evidence.source: CNO email to Vice President of Operations (2026-10-23)
evidence.text: "Until the travel nurses arrive I want the 4 West huddle paused. It ties up the 4 West charge nurse for half an hour every morning and I'd rather float her to the ED for the afternoon crunch. The pilot is a nice idea but the ED is where the problem is."

hypotheses.text: ED nurse understaffing is the main cause of the rise in ED length of stay for admitted patients.
Most of the rise is longer boarding of admitted patients, driven by later inpatient discharges on the hospitalist-covered medical wards since the March 2026 rounding change.
A rise in ED visit volume or patient acuity is the main cause of the longer ED length of stay.
A reduction in inpatient bed capacity (fewer staffed beds or higher overall occupancy) is the main cause of the longer boarding times.
The September 2026 reduction in evening bed-cleaning staff is adding materially to ED boarding time.

edges.from: ED registered-nurse staffing hours per visit
edges.to: ED length of stay for admitted patients

edges.from: March 2026 hospitalist rounding change (09:30 start, new admissions first)
edges.to: Later inpatient discharge times on medical wards

edges.from: Earlier inpatient discharge (discharges completed before noon)
edges.to: Shorter ED boarding time for patients admitted to that ward
Longer door-to-provider time and more patients leaving without being seen

actions.text: Extend the early-discharge huddle (charge nurse, case manager, rounding hospitalist; likely discharges seen before the new-admission round) to the other three hospitalist-covered medical wards, keeping the 08:00 meeting, and track before-noon discharges and boarding time weekly.
Open a staffed discharge lounge where patients who already have discharge orders can wait for transport, freeing their beds sooner.
Restore evening bed-cleaning staffing to six attendants as the hospital's primary fix for ED boarding.
Approve the $1.46M travel-nurse contract for the ED, funded by deferring the two vacant medical-ward case manager positions as proposed.
Pause the 4 West early-discharge huddle and float the 4 West charge nurse to the ED during afternoon peaks until travel nurses arrive.

evidenceRequests.text: Bed turnaround (dirty-to-clean) times by hour of day, July-October 2026, reconstructed from the new EVS system
Monthly and hourly door-to-provider and left-without-being-seen rates, January-October 2026, aligned to the 1 May triage-provider change
Exit-interview themes from ED nurses who resigned in 2025-2026
ED length-of-stay benchmarks for peer community hospitals in the state
Hospitalist patient census per physician per day, before and after March 2026
